newsitem.title: USA: AOL, CompuServe still talking but deal not imminent.
newsitem.headline: AOL, CompuServe still talking but deal not imminent.

text.p: America Online Inc. and CompuServe Corp. are still in merger discussions, although the scope of the talks has changed to include other parties and selling CompuServe in pieces, industry sources said Sunday.

No deal is imminent and the recent introduction of legislation that would prevent certain types of tax-free mergers could also be having an impact on the talks. But H&R Block Inc, which owns 80 percent of CompuServe, is hoping to get a deal done before its fiscal year ends this month, sources said.
"It may happen with different people or it may happen in bits and pieces," said one industry executive. "It's hard to say how it will all end up."

A CompuServe spokesman in Columbus, Ohio, said that the online service is still in talks to sell the company, but he declined to identify the possible acquiror or acquirors, or to comment any further. An AOL spokeswoman in Dulles, Va., also declined to comment.

Sources have said that America Online has been in talks to buy its online rival in an all-stock transaction, valued at about $1.1 billion to $.1.2 billion. Because of AOL's low cash position, it has been trying to do a stock deal, but one industry source said that this was one of the many sticking points for H&R Block, because AOL's stock has been very volatile and a deal would be dilutive.

"There have been late night sessions and ongoing meetings and so forth, but there are difficulties in getting a deal together," said one executive close to CompuServe. "Everything under the sun and the moon is under consideration."
AOL has been looking at CompuServe in an effort to boost its subscriber base in its goal to reach 10 million subscribers, and increase its corporate and international businesses.

Some analysts have said AOL also wants to add more capacity to its network, which has had problems meeting the surge in demand since it went to flat-rate pricing. But David Simons, managing director of Digital Video Investments, pointed to an agreement on Thursday between AOL and BBN Corp, to extend BBN's contract in building AOLnet to more than $700 million over four years.
"This implies that an acquisition of CompuServe is not imminent for the purposes of network expansion," Simons said.

While Wall Street analysts have mostly been opposed to the world's largest online service buying CompuServe outright, the prospect of it buying pieces, such as its corporate network business or its international customers, struck a better chord with some analysts.
"There is no great scenario I can see where they would want to buy the consumer service," said Abhishek Gami, an analyst with Nesbitt Burns Securities, referring to CompuServe's flagship CSI service.
"I believe they would be most interested in buying the Network Services business ... But CompuServe doesn't want to lose that gem without getting rid of the rest," Gami said.

AOL has been trying to expand corporate usage of its network. CompuServe's Network Services business, which is its portion of its network used by corporate customers, was about 31 percent of its total revenues in its third fiscal quarter and analysts have said it is CompuServe's best asset.

Gami also pointed out that AOL may have a hard time buying CompuServe's international business, because it would have to get the partners in its own international ventures, Bertelsmann AG in Germany and Mitsui & Co. in Japan, to buy out its international subscribers in its European and Japanese ventures.

"AOL would have to figure out a way for their joint venture partners to buy the subscribers outright," Gami said. "Based on the current (subscriber) valuation, that would overwhelm the cost of the ventures."

It could not be immediately learned what other companies CompuServe was talking with as part of a possible three-way deal. But analysts said that some of the baby bell companies, long distance telephone companies and Internet access providers would be good candidates to buy the flagship CSI service, because they represent a loyal subscriber base that has not switched to AOL.

Some industry sources said that legislation just introduced Friday in Congress to block a type of merger known as a Morris Trust deal is hurting the ongoing AOL/CompuServe talks because tax preparation giant H&R Block was considering such a tax- free, stock-for-stock deal to sell CompuServe.

In a Morris Trust, a company creates a subsidiary to hold the businesses it wants to keep and leaving behind the businesses it wants to sell. Then the businesses that are acquired are purchased in a tax-free, stock-for-stock deal.
But analysts said now that the proposed legislation is clouding the landscape for these kind of deals.

For example, on Friday, when AirTouch Communications said it would buy the U.S. cellular properties from US West Media Group in a deal valued at about $5 billion in stock and assumed debt, it said that the proposed Morris Trust legislation would block their deal, if such legislation passes without any modifications.

One industry executive who asked not to be identified also pointed out that it would be difficult to sell the online service in parts, because it has fixed costs spread across two businsesses. "I think it's going to be very difficult to put together a deal that deals with parts of the business," the executive said.
